h: Drawing offices, a dry dock and a shipyard ride
p: Inside, the galleries are full of clever touches. A ride carries you through a recreation of the shipyard, with the sights and sounds of riveters at work high up on the gantry, which gives a real sense of how dangerous and noisy the job must have been. Later sections recreate the ship's cabins in different classes, so you can compare the luxury of first class with the more basic quarters further down.

Just outside, the outline of the slipways where Titanic and her sister Olympic were built is marked out on the ground, and the sheer scale is breathtaking. A short walk away, the Thompson Graving Dock, the giant dry dock where Titanic had her final fitting-out, is a sight in its own right. You can also see the old Harland and Wolff headquarters, where the ships were designed in elegant drawing offices; the building is now a hotel, and some of the original rooms are open to guests and diners.

Allow around two to three hours for Titanic Belfast itself, plus extra if you're adding the SS Nomadic, which is the last remaining White Star Line ship and once ferried passengers out to Titanic in Cherbourg.

There's plenty more in the area. Titanic Studios nearby is where a lot of a famous fantasy TV series was filmed, and W5, a science centre for kids, is a short walk away at the arena complex. Head back along the river and you'll find the Big Fish, a colourful sculpture covered in tiles that tell the story of Belfast, near the Lagan Weir.
